newsitem.title: FRANCE: French prosecutor urges jail for crash pilot.
newsitem.headline: French prosecutor urges jail for crash pilot.

text.p: A French public prosecutor called on Tuesday for the pilot of an Airbus plane which crashed on a demonstration flight in 1988, killing three people and injuring 50, to be jailed for manslaughter.

Prosecutor Rene Pech requested a "particularly severe" prison term against pilot Michel Asseline, who has denied flying recklessly and blamed the accident on engine failure and design errors. The maximum penalty is two years' imprisonment.
"He is an irresponsible daredevil who wanted out of pride to impress the oublic and also have fun for himself," Pech said.
He said Asseline was "principally responsible" for the disaster.

Pech also requested a jail term long enough to escape an automatic amnesty against co-pilot Pierre Mazieres, and lesser suspended sentences against Air France executives Henri Petit and Jacques Gauthier and the organiser of the air show Francois Furstenberger.
Minor sentences would be covered by an amnesty declared by President Jacques Chirac last year to mark his election, since the disaster took place before that.
The A-320 plane, manufactured by the European Airbus consortium, crashed into a forest adjoining an airfield at Habsheim in eastern France after flying too low on June 26, 1988.

Air France operations chief Petit is accused of breaking a ban on such flights carrying passengers and letting the plane fly lower under the 170-ft (30 metres) minimum altitude allowed in air shows, even though there were high trees at the end of the runway.
Asseline and Mazieres blamed the crash on the engines, the computer system and the controls.

Pech rejected Asseline's charges that French authorities tampered with the flight recorder to hide faults at a time when the plane was being launched on the market. He said it was "an absolute scientific certainty" that the recorder had not been tampered with.
Airbus is a consortium made up of France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Construcciones Aeronauticas SA of Spain and the Daimler-Benz Aerospace unit of Germany's Daimler-Benz AG.
